newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco officials discussed hiding data - reports.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco officials discussed hiding data - reports.

text.p: Tobacco company officials and researchers discussed the need to destroy or hide sensitive documents such as internal reports on the addictive nature of tobacco, U.S. newspapers reported on Wednesday.

The Washington Post and Los Angeles Times quoted memos cited in new court filings by the state of Minnesota and Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota, which are seeking to force tobacco companies to reimburse them for Medicaid costs.

The Washington Post quoted attorneys involved with the lawsuit as saying they found "an extraordinary array of evidence of destruction" or "partial destruction" of papers dealing with scientific research by tobacco firms.
The new filings discuss Philip Morris Cos Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., and Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., a unit of B.A.T. Industries Plc.
The Los Angeles Times said Philip Morris officials suggested that internal documents about sensitive research conducted at a German laboratory be destroyed.

The Post also cited one Philip Morris document written by nicotine researcher William Dunn and addressed to Thomas Osdene, Philip Morris director of research form 1969 until 1984 and concerns a study Dunn approved about nicotine's possible addictive effects.

If the researcher "is able to demonstrate, as she anticipates, no withdrawal effects of nicotine, we will want to pursue this avenue with some vigor," Dunn wrote. "If, however, the results with nicotine are similar to those gotten with morphine and caffeine, we will want to bury it," the Post quoted the memo as saying.
The paper said it reached Dunn at his home and he said the comment about burying research was "not written in all seriousness."
